card.title: Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Parallel wires feel F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π r) because each sits in the other's field. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite currents repel. The old definition of the ampere is this force at 1 m separation.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Governing equation for "Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors" — state with units, then use in one numerical.
F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π r)
Same direction: attraction

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ state the rule without its limit → ✅ note when it applies / stops applying.  ·  ❌ no diagram → ✅ add one labelled figure / structured list.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: μ0 / 2π = 2 × 10^−7.  ·  Multiply by length to get the force on a piece.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: A long straight wire produces circles of magnetic field. A second wire, parallel to the first, carries current across that field and feels a force F = I L B sinθ. With the wires parallel, θ is 90°.  ·  Substituting B = μ0 I1 /(2π r) gives the force per unit length F/L = μ0 I1 I2 /(2π r). The force is mutual: each wire feels the same magnitude.

rows.label: Limitation

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: • Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors  ·  Each wire sits in the other's field.  ·  Parallel currents in the same direction attract.  ·  Opposite currents repel.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: answer pattern for "Force between two parallel current-carrying conductors": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: What separation and currents define the old standard force?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Two long parallel wires carry 2.0 A and 3.0 A in the same direction. Their separation is 0.10 m. Find the force per unit length and say whether they attract. Use μ0 / 2π = 2.0 × 10^−7.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Parallel currents in the same direction → A  ·  Opposite currents → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: If the currents are in the same direction the force is attractive. If they are in opposite directions the force is repulsive. The right-hand rule on one wire's field, then on the force, gives this.  ·  The ampere was historically defined from this force: two long parallel wires, 1 m apart, carrying 1 A each, attract with 2 × 10^−7 N per metre of length.  ·  The wires must be long compared with their separation, or the formula is only a middle-region estimate. The field is not uniform, but the result above is already the integrated force on a straight parallel wire.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The force per unit length is the definition behind the ampere.  ·  Same direction attracts. It is not the same rule as like charges.  ·  The formula is force per unit length, not the force on a named length until you multiply.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The wires are not point charges.  ·  State the current directions before attraction or repulsion.  ·  Keep F and F/L distinct.

rows.label: More ideas
